title: Your daily rule
hookLine: write morning, midday, evening and night in one page
tomorrow: the rest commandment appears twice, with two reasons. which is it?

cards: Habit apps let you add as many goals as you like, and twelve on the first day feels brave. Here's a story that runs the other way.

The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, is taken up through the heavens on the Mi'raj, the ascent on the night of the Night Journey. There, the hadith says, God enjoins fifty prayers a day on his community.
On the way down he passes Moses, who asks what he was given. Fifty, he says. Go back, says Moses.
Your people won't be able to bear it.

teach.h: MOSES: YOUR PEOPLE CAN'T BEAR IT.
teach.b: So he goes back, and the number comes down.

Moses sends him back again, and again, until it reaches five, and God says the line that solves the puzzle: these are five, and they are fifty. My word doesn't change. Even then Moses says: still too many, go back.
And the Prophet says: I have asked my Lord until I am shy to ask again. Two strange things, two answers. Why would Moses push for less?

teach.h: A RULE A HUMAN DAY CAN CARRY.
teach.b: In one telling he says why: he had tested people before, the Children of Israel, and he knew what a human day can carry. A rule that breaks people isn't a rule; it's a wall. And how are five also fifty?
In the hadith, the reward of the fifty stays. The five are kept, and kept, they count as the whole.
This is why Muslims pray salat five times a day: Fajr at dawn, Dhuhr at midday, Asr in the afternoon, Maghrib at sunset, and Isha at night.
Five doors in the day, each one small enough to walk through, and each one opening onto God.
Told this way, the story is mercy, not a discount on devotion. That's the shape of a daily rule: a page you can keep, not a list that wins on day one and is gone by day four.

how: Muslims pray the five daily prayers, Fajr, Dhuhr, Asr, Maghrib and Isha, at set times from dawn to night; the hadith of the Night Journey tells how the five were given.

o: a long list of goals for being more productive
a page of a few practices across your whole day
a strict timetable for every hour you're awake

games.q: fifty become five: tap the pairs.
p: the Prophet's journey through the heavens
go back: your people can't bear it

s: in the hadith, the daily prayers were five from the start
God first enjoined fifty; Moses sent the Prophet back until it was five.
Moses argued for fewer prayers, not more
he said the people could not bear fifty, and kept sending the Prophet back.
fewer prayers meant less reward in the story
'these are five, and they are fifty.'

games.q: your friend set out to read a whole scripture in a month and is behind on day four. what does the Night Journey story suggest?
o: a smaller daily portion she can actually keep, and let it count.
double tomorrow's reading so she catches back up.
quit, since falling behind shows rules don't work for her.
games.why: Moses pushed fifty down to five because people couldn't bear fifty, and the five were counted as fifty.

practice: Take a page and write four words down the side: morning, midday, evening, night. Beside each, write one small practice from these weeks, only one. Read the page once, slowly, and breathe as if the day were already in order.

wordCard.voice: Your daily rule: one page that sets a few small practices across morning, midday, evening and night, few enough to keep.

orig.note: Arabic: the ritual prayer Muslims say five times a day.

carryVoice: Keep this one: my day, on one page, small enough to keep. That's the daily practice, gathered.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 349 (Abu Dharr: the ascent; fifty prayers enjoined; Moses sends the Prophet back; reduced to five; 'they are five and they are fifty; my word does not change')
Sahih al-Bukhari 3207 (Malik ibn Sa'sa'a: the same account; 'I have asked my Lord until I feel shy')
